why_how.text: Picking the right class keeps you legal, because each class covers a specific kind of vehicle.
Mopeds and motorcycles follow different rules, so knowing them avoids riding without the right license.

scenario.text: Dana drives a car daily and is thinking about buying a heavy motor home that tows a small trailer.

reasoning.text: The car is a passenger vehicle under the Class D weight limit, but the motor home with a trailer is a heavy combination.

result.text: Dana keeps Class D for the car and would need Class F for the heavy motor home pulling a trailer.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a big-looking vehicle always needs a heavier class.

correction.text: The weight rating, not the vehicle's look, decides which class you need.

memory_support.text: D for daily, E for one heavy unit, F for heavy combinations, G for mopeds, M for motorcycles.

prompt.text: A non-commercial motor home over the Class D weight limit tows nothing. Which class covers it?

answer.text: Class E, because it is a heavy single unit.

rationale.text: Class E covers single-unit vehicles above the Class D limit, while Class F is for combinations.

lines.text: Classes D, E, F, G and M
Weight and combination decide the class

narration.text: South Carolina sorts non-commercial drivers into five license classes, and the right one depends on what you drive. Class D covers ordinary passenger vehicles such as cars and trucks up to twenty-six thousand pounds gross vehicle weight. Above that weight, Class E covers single heavy vehicles and Class F covers heavy combinations. Class G is the moped license, and Class M covers motorcycles and three-wheel vehicles. In this lesson you will learn to place any vehicle in its class, which matters because driving outside your class is not allowed.

lines.text: Class D stops at the weight limit
Looks do not decide the class

narration.text: The key idea for Class D is weight. Class D is limited to non-commercial passenger vehicles weighing no more than twenty-six thousand pounds gross vehicle weight. A vehicle can look large and still fit in Class D, or look ordinary and be rated above the limit. The manual is clear that the weight rating, not the vehicle's look, decides which class you need. So before you judge a truck or motor home by its size, check its rating. That single number tells you whether you stay in Class D or move to a heavier class. Weight rating first, appearance never.

lines.text: Class F: heavy vehicle plus trailer

narration.text: Once a non-commercial vehicle is rated above twenty-six thousand pounds, the question becomes whether it is one unit or a combination. Class E covers single-unit vehicles above that weight, such as big trucks and motor homes. Class F covers combinations above that weight, such as a truck or motor home pulling a trailer or another vehicle. Both classes share the same weight threshold, so the only difference is the hitch. One heavy vehicle on its own points to Class E, and the same heavy vehicle towing something points to Class F.

lines.text: Class G: moped license at fifteen

narration.text: Class G is the moped license. Its minimum age is fifteen, and only the vision and knowledge tests are required. If you already hold a valid license or permit in any of the other four classes, you need no separate license to ride a moped. Class D, E and F holders may also operate a moped or a three-wheel vehicle, but not a two-wheel motorcycle with a detachable sidecar. Class M covers two-wheel motorcycles, with or without a sidecar, and three-wheel vehicles. A rider who drives both a motorcycle and another vehicle gets one license endorsed for both.

lines.text: A moped needs no extra license
A two-wheel motorcycle always needs M

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because any valid license already covers a moped, some drivers assume their car license also covers a motorcycle. It does not. A moped needs no separate license for someone who holds another valid license or permit, while a two-wheel motorcycle always needs Class M. If you plan to drive both a motorcycle and another type of vehicle, you pass driving tests for both and receive one license endorsed for two classifications. Keep the line clear in your mind: mopeds ride free on your license, motorcycles never do.

Here is a quick check: a non-commercial motor home is rated above twenty-six thousand pounds gross vehicle weight, and it is not towing anything. Which class covers it? The answer is Class E. Class E is for single-unit vehicles above the Class D weight limit, and this motor home is a single unit. If the same motor home were pulling a trailer, it would become a heavy combination and need Class F instead. Remember that weight takes you out of Class D, and the hitch decides between Class E and Class F. The hitch is the whole difference between those two heavy classes.

lines.text: D daily, E one heavy unit
F heavy combination, G moped, M motorcycle

narration.text: To close, picture the five classes as a ladder. Class D is everyday driving up to twenty-six thousand pounds. Class E is one heavy vehicle above that weight, and Class F is a heavy vehicle towing something. Class G is the moped license, which you do not need if you already hold another valid license, and Class M covers motorcycles and three-wheel vehicles. Use the weight rating, not looks, and ask whether there is a hitch. Those two questions place almost any non-commercial vehicle in the right class. Those two questions are the fastest way to answer any class question.

why_how.text: Commercial classes are set by weight, towing and use, so mixing them up leads to driving without the right license.
Every driver must carry the right documents and may hold only one license.

scenario.text: Sam drives a bus built for twenty passengers that is not heavy enough for Class A or B.

reasoning.text: Class C covers vehicles outside A and B that are designed for sixteen or more people counting the driver.

result.text: Sam needs a Class C commercial license, defined by the bus's use rather than its weight.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking every commercial class is defined by weight.

correction.text: Class C is defined by use: vehicles built for sixteen or more occupants or placarded for hazardous materials.

memory_support.text: A tows heavy, B is one heavy unit, C carries crowds or hazards.

prompt.text: A single heavy truck tows a small trailer of only a few thousand pounds. Which commercial class fits it?

answer.text: Class B, because it is one heavy vehicle towing no more than ten thousand pounds.

rationale.text: Class A applies only when the towed unit is rated over ten thousand pounds.

narration.text: Commercial licenses come in three classes, and each is defined in its own way. Class A covers heavy combinations, Class B covers heavy single vehicles, and Class C covers vehicles defined by what they carry. This unit also covers two rules that apply to every driver, commercial or not: you may hold only one license, and you must carry the right documents whenever you drive. Even if you never plan to drive a truck or bus, these rules help you understand how the license system fits together. We start with Class A and Class B, which are both built around heavy weight ratings.

lines.text: Class A: heavy combination, heavy trailer
Class B: heavy single vehicle, light towing

narration.text: Class A and Class B both start at a rating of twenty-six thousand and one pounds or more. A Class A license covers vehicle combinations with that combined rating when the towed unit is rated over ten thousand pounds. A Class B license covers a single vehicle with that rating, including one towing no more than ten thousand pounds. So the towed unit's rating is the dividing line. A heavy truck pulling a light trailer stays in Class B, while the same truck pulling a heavy trailer moves to Class A. The truck itself is heavy in both cases; only the trailer changes the class.

lines.text: Sixteen or more people, counting the driver

narration.text: Class C works differently. It covers vehicles that fit neither Class A nor Class B but are designed to carry sixteen or more people counting the driver, or are placarded for hazardous materials. In other words, Class C is defined by use, not weight. A passenger van built for a large group, or a smaller vehicle carrying placarded hazardous materials, can need a commercial license even when it is far lighter than Class A or B vehicles. Ask what the vehicle is built to carry before you decide. That is why passenger capacity and hazard placards matter as much as weight here.

lines.text: Not every commercial class is about weight
Class C turns on passengers or hazards

narration.text: A common trap is assuming that every commercial class is decided by weight alone. That works for Class A and Class B, but not for Class C. Class C is defined by use: vehicles built for sixteen or more occupants including the driver, or placarded for hazardous materials, when they are not Class A or B. If you only check the weight rating, you could miss that a lighter passenger vehicle still needs a commercial license. Always add a second question about what the vehicle is designed to carry. Weight is only half the picture when a vehicle carries people or hazards.

lines.text: Only one valid license per driver

narration.text: Each qualified driver holds just one license, endorsed for one or more classes, and having more than one valid license is illegal. When you are behind the wheel, you must have three things: a valid license, the vehicle registration and a valid insurance card for that class of vehicle. If you cannot show them, you can be fined. Keep the registration and insurance card in the vehicle and your license with you every time you drive, so a routine stop never turns into a fine. One license, endorsed for every class you hold, is the rule for everyone.

Here is a quick check: a single heavy truck rated over twenty-six thousand pounds is towing a trailer rated at only a few thousand pounds. Which commercial class fits? The answer is Class B. Class B covers a heavy single vehicle, including one towing no more than ten thousand pounds. Class A would apply only if the towed unit were rated over ten thousand pounds. The truck's own weight puts it in commercial territory, and the trailer's rating decides between Class B and Class A. Check the towed unit, and the choice between the two classes becomes clear.

lines.text: A tows heavy, B is one heavy unit

narration.text: To wrap up, Class A is the heavy combination class, used when the towed unit is rated over ten thousand pounds. Class B is the heavy single vehicle, which may tow up to ten thousand pounds. Class C is defined by use: sixteen or more people counting the driver, or placarded hazardous materials. Across all classes, a driver holds only one license, and every trip requires a valid license, the registration and a valid insurance card. Keep these rules straight and the commercial classes become easy to sort. Those few rules cover every commercial class question in this section.

why_how.text: The beginner's permit is the first step for every new driver, and its rules decide when and with whom you may drive.
Logging the right practice and waiting the full period keeps a teen on track for a license.

result.text: If the cousin is twenty-two, licensed for years and sits up front, Riley may practice, and the hours count toward the forty.

correction.text: After midnight the supervisor must be a licensed person from the list in the state code.

narration.text: Every new driver in South Carolina begins in the same place. You gather documents, apply, and receive a beginner's permit that lets you practice under supervision. In this unit you will learn which documents to bring, who qualifies for a permit, when you may drive with it, who may sit beside you, how much practice a teen must log, and the earliest day you may apply for a license. These rules shape the first six months of your driving life, so it pays to know them well before you take the wheel. Each rule builds on the one before it, so take them in order.

A United States citizen applying for a first permit, license or identification card brings original documents that prove citizenship, identity, birth date and birthplace, Social Security number and South Carolina address, as listed on form MV-ninety-three. An applicant who is not a United States citizen applies at a branch that processes international customers and follows the checklist on form MV-ninety-four. Checking the right form before your visit saves a second trip, because the branch needs originals, not copies, to prove who you are and where you live.

lines.text: Age fifteen, vision and knowledge tests
Drive six in the morning to midnight
Supervisor at least twenty-one, one year licensed

narration.text: Anyone who has never held a driver's license starts with a beginner's permit. You must be at least fifteen and pass the vision and knowledge tests. With the permit you may drive from six in the morning until midnight, as long as a licensed driver sits in the front seat who is at least twenty-one and has at least one year of driving experience. Driving after midnight is a separate case with stricter supervision. Treat the permit as a learning license: every mile is practice with an experienced driver right beside you.

Many families assume the same supervisor rule applies around the clock. It does not. During the day and evening, a licensed driver at least twenty-one with one year of experience may supervise. After midnight, permit driving needs supervision by a licensed person from the list in the state code, section fifty-six dash one dash one hundred. That list is narrower than any adult over twenty-one, so a trusted friend who qualifies at nine at night may not qualify at one in the morning. Check the list before any late trip.

A permit holder who is fifteen or sixteen must practice at least forty hours, ten of them at night, beside an approved supervisor such as a father, mother or legal guardian. The approved list also includes a person approved in writing by the Department of Social Services, with a copy sent to the SCDMV, and ends with a responsible adult who accepts the duties in the law and has notarized written permission from a parent, guardian or custodian. The earliest you may apply for any license is the one hundred eighty-first day after getting the permit.

Here is a quick check: a fifteen-year-old permit holder is logging supervised practice. Of the forty required hours, how many must take place at night? The answer is at least ten. Permit holders aged fifteen or sixteen must practice at least forty hours in total, with ten of those hours at night, beside an approved supervisor such as a parent or legal guardian. Night practice matters because conditions after dark are different, and the requirement makes sure a new driver has real experience with them before driving alone.

To close, a first-time driver brings the right original documents, then gets a beginner's permit at fifteen or older after passing the vision and knowledge tests. The permit allows driving from six in the morning to midnight with a licensed driver at least twenty-one with a year of experience, and only a listed supervisor after midnight. Teens log forty hours, ten at night, with an approved supervisor. The earliest day to apply for any license is the one hundred eighty-first day after the permit, or any day after that.

why_how.text: The route to a first license depends on age, so teens and adults need different checklists.
Missing one teen requirement, such as the PDLA form, can delay a license.

result.text: Morgan brings the PDLA form from the driver's education program to show those requirements are met.

correction.text: A first-time applicant aged seventeen or older must also hold a permit for more than one hundred eighty days before the skills test.

title.text: Two routes to a first license

lines.text: Adults: wait out the permit period

narration.text: Once you hold a beginner's permit, the path to a first license depends on your age. Adults aged seventeen or older mainly need to hold the permit long enough. Teens aged fifteen or sixteen have a longer checklist that includes driver's education, school requirements and logged practice. In this unit you will learn exactly what each group must show before the skills test, and which form brings the teen requirements together. Knowing the list ahead of time keeps a test appointment from being wasted on missing paperwork.

lines.text: Permit held more than one hundred eighty days

narration.text: A first-time applicant who is seventeen or older must have held a beginner's permit for more than one hundred eighty days before taking the skills test for full privileges. This waiting period applies even though adults skip the teen program's extra requirements. It gives every new driver at least half a year of supervised practice before driving alone. So an adult who gets a permit cannot simply take the skills test the next week. Plan for the full waiting period and use it to practice the skills the test will check.

lines.text: Driver's education: eight plus six hours

narration.text: A first-time applicant aged fifteen or sixteen needs more than one hundred eighty days on the permit plus several other items. Driver's education must be completed, with eight hours in the classroom and six hours of driving. The teen must be enrolled in school, not suspended or expelled, and have satisfactory attendance. And the practice hours logged on the permit must be complete. Each piece is required, so a teen who finishes driver's education but has poor school attendance is still not ready to apply for a license.

lines.text: Myth: adults can skip the wait
Truth: more than one hundred eighty days

narration.text: A common myth says that adults can skip the permit wait because they are old enough to drive alone. That is not true. A first-time applicant aged seventeen or older must hold the beginner's permit for more than one hundred eighty days before the skills test for full privileges. What adults skip are the teen extras, such as driver's education hours, school attendance rules and the PDLA form. The waiting period itself applies to every first-time applicant, so count your days before you book the test. Every first-time applicant, whatever the age, waits out that period.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old is signing up for driver's education to meet the first license requirements. How many classroom hours and how many driving hours must the course include? The answer is eight hours in the classroom and six hours of driving. These hours are separate from the forty hours of supervised permit practice. Once the course is passed, the program hands out the PDLA form, which the teen submits to show driver's education, school attendance and practice are complete. Keep the classroom hours and the practice hours separate in your mind.

lines.text: Adults: permit more than one hundred eighty days
Teens: driver's ed, school, practice, PDLA

narration.text: To close, every first-time applicant waits out the permit period of more than one hundred eighty days. Adults aged seventeen or older need little more before the skills test. Teens aged fifteen or sixteen must also complete driver's education with eight classroom hours and six driving hours, be enrolled in school without suspension or expulsion and with satisfactory attendance, and finish their logged practice. The PDLA form, handed out by the driver's education program after the course, ties the teen requirements together for the branch.

why_how.text: The graduated stages limit when and with whom a teen may drive, so knowing the limits keeps a young driver legal.
Points in the first year can suspend a young driver's license.

reasoning.text: During daylight saving time, solo driving on a conditional license runs until eight in the evening.

result.text: Jamie may drive alone to the seven o'clock practice in July, but in standard time solo driving ends at six.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking solo driving on a conditional license always ends at six in the evening.

correction.text: Solo driving ends at six in standard time but at eight during daylight saving time.

memory_support.text: Fifteen and a half for conditional, sixteen for special restricted, two young passengers at most.

prompt.text: During standard time, when does solo driving on a conditional license end?

rationale.text: A conditional licensee may drive alone from six in the morning to six in the evening, or until eight during daylight saving time.

lines.text: For drivers aged fifteen to seventeen

narration.text: South Carolina's graduated driver's license program serves drivers aged fifteen to seventeen. It limits night and unsupervised driving at first, then eases those limits over time as the driver gains experience. In this unit you will meet the two teen stages, the conditional license and the special restricted license, and learn who qualifies for each, when they may drive alone, how many young passengers they may carry, and what happens if they collect points. These rules are among the most tested details for teen drivers, so learn each limit precisely.

lines.text: At least fifteen and a half, under sixteen

narration.text: The conditional license is open to applicants who are at least fifteen and a half but under sixteen and who pass the vision and skills tests. A conditional licensee may drive alone from six in the morning to six in the evening, or until eight in the evening during daylight saving time. From then until midnight, the teen may drive with a licensed driver aged twenty-one or older. A conditional licensee earns full privileges after holding the license for one year with no traffic offenses and no at-fault collisions. That clean year is one of two routes out of the conditional stage.

lines.text: Sixteen but under seventeen, vision and skills
Or sixteen with a conditional license

narration.text: The special restricted license is for applicants who are sixteen but under seventeen and pass the vision and skills tests, or who are sixteen and already hold a conditional license. That second route means the two teen stages follow one another: a teen who starts with a conditional license can move to the special restricted license at sixteen. Both stages share the same limits on late-night driving and passengers, which the next slides explain. Keep the age windows straight: fifteen and a half for conditional, sixteen for special restricted.

lines.text: At most two passengers under twenty-one
Midnight to six: listed supervisor only

narration.text: Conditional and special restricted licensees may carry at most two passengers under twenty-one, unless a licensed adult aged twenty-one or older rides along. Family members and students being carried to and from school are the exception. From midnight to six in the morning, these teen drivers may drive only when supervised by a licensed person from the list in the state code. And a driver under seventeen who collects six or more points before holding the license for one year has it suspended for six months, so careful driving protects the license itself.

lines.text: Daylight saving time: solo until eight

narration.text: Here is a trap that catches many families. They remember that solo driving on a conditional license ends at six in the evening and apply that rule all year. In fact, solo driving ends at six in standard time but at eight during daylight saving time. A teen who drives alone at seven in the evening in December is breaking the rule, while the same trip in July is allowed. Whatever the season, from the solo cutoff until midnight the teen needs a licensed driver aged twenty-one or older in the car. Check the calendar before every solo evening drive, and the rule stays easy.

Here is a quick check: it is November, so standard time applies, and a conditional licensee wants to drive alone. When does solo driving end? The answer is six in the evening. A conditional licensee may drive alone from six in the morning to six in the evening in standard time, or until eight during daylight saving time. After the solo cutoff and until midnight, a licensed driver aged twenty-one or older must ride along. Getting the season right is what makes this question easy. Season first, then the clock, and you will get this question right every time.

lines.text: Conditional at fifteen and a half

narration.text: To close, the graduated program covers ages fifteen to seventeen and loosens its limits over time. The conditional license starts at fifteen and a half after the vision and skills tests, with solo driving until six or, in daylight saving time, eight in the evening. The special restricted license follows at sixteen. Both allow at most two passengers under twenty-one without a licensed adult, need a listed supervisor from midnight to six, and six points in the first year bring a six-month suspension for a driver under seventeen.

why_how.text: A waiver lets a teen work or join activities later in the evening, within a firm limit.
Full privileges remove the teen limits, and two routes lead there.

scenario.text: Taylor, sixteen with a special restricted license, works a shift that ends at eleven at night.

reasoning.text: A waiver lets a sixteen-year-old drive alone until midnight for work, but never after midnight.

result.text: Taylor brings the two letters and the forms to a branch, applies for the waiver, and may then drive home alone before midnight.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a work waiver allows driving at any hour.

correction.text: A waiver extends solo driving to midnight, yet driving after midnight is still not allowed under it.

memory_support.text: Waiver to midnight, never past; full privileges at seventeen or after a clean year.

prompt.text: Which two letters does a waiver application need?

answer.text: A letter from the school, church, work or activity explaining the need, and a letter from a parent or legal guardian approving it.

rationale.text: The waiver needs both letters, along with the forms, a vision test and the fee.

narration.text: This unit covers two ways teen limits change. First, a sixteen-year-old with a special restricted or conditional license may get a waiver to drive alone later in the evening for work or certain activities. Second, every teen driver eventually reaches full privileges, either by age or by a clean driving year. You will learn what a waiver allows, what it takes to apply, when full privileges arrive and what the SCDMV sends you when they do. These details answer the questions teens and parents face as schedules get busier.

A sixteen-year-old with a special restricted or conditional license may get a waiver to drive alone until midnight for work or certain extracurricular activities. The waiver stops there. Driving after midnight is never allowed under it. So a teen whose shift ends at eleven can drive home alone with a waiver, but a teen whose activity ends at half past midnight cannot drive alone under the waiver. Plan schedules around that firm limit, and remember that the waiver is about later hours, not about removing the other teen rules.

Applying for a waiver takes a branch visit. You bring form four-forty-seven-NC and the Consent for Minor form, four-forty-seven-CM, signed by a qualified adult in front of SCDMV staff. You also bring two letters: one from the school, church, work or activity explaining the need, and one from a parent or legal guardian approving the waiver and explaining why. A vision test is part of the visit, and there is a twenty-five dollar fee. Gather everything before you go so the waiver can be issued in one trip. Missing any one of these items can mean a second trip to the branch.

The trap with waivers is believing that a good reason, such as a job, makes any hour legal. It does not. A waiver extends a sixteen-year-old's solo driving to midnight for work or certain activities, yet driving after midnight is still not allowed under it. If a shift or event runs past midnight, the teen needs another plan, such as a ride or a qualifying supervisor. Treat midnight as a wall that no waiver can move, and the rule becomes simple to follow. No reason, however good, moves that limit for a teen on a waiver.

lines.text: At seventeen, or after a clean year
Keep the license in the sleeve

narration.text: Full privileges arrive at seventeen, or after a year on a conditional or special restricted license with no traffic offenses and no at-fault collisions. No branch visit is needed. If the year is not clean, turning seventeen is the other route. Once you reach full privileges, the SCDMV mails you a sleeve, and you must keep the license inside it to use those full privileges. That sleeve is the visible sign that the teen limits no longer apply, so do not set it aside. Until that sleeve arrives, the teen limits still apply to every drive.

Here is a quick check: a sixteen-year-old is gathering paperwork for a waiver to drive home from a part-time job. Besides the forms, the vision test and the fee, which two letters are needed? The answer is a letter from the school, church, work or activity explaining the need, and a letter from a parent or legal guardian approving the waiver and explaining why. Both letters are required. With them and the forms, the branch can issue a waiver that allows solo driving until midnight, never after. Two letters, two forms, a vision test and the fee complete the request.

lines.text: Full privileges: seventeen or clean year

narration.text: To close, a waiver lets a sixteen-year-old with a special restricted or conditional license drive alone until midnight for work or certain activities, but never after midnight. Applying takes a branch visit with the two forms, two letters, a vision test and a twenty-five dollar fee. Full privileges arrive at seventeen, or after a year with no traffic offenses and no at-fault collisions, with no branch visit needed. When they do, the SCDMV mails a sleeve, and the license must stay inside it. With these rules, a busy teen schedule can still stay within the law.

why_how.text: Knowing which tests you face, and the rules for taking them, keeps a test visit from ending in failure.
The moped license is the one first license with a shorter test list.

scenario.text: Alex is taking the knowledge test and feels a phone buzz in a pocket.

reasoning.text: Bringing any electronic device into the test, or talking to anyone, fails the knowledge test.

result.text: Alex should leave the phone outside before starting, because having it in the test area means failing.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a quick question to another person during the knowledge test is harmless.

correction.text: Talking to anyone during the knowledge test is one of the actions that fail it.

memory_support.text: Vision, knowledge, skills for every first license, except the moped, which skips skills.

prompt.text: Which first license needs no skills test?

rationale.text: Every first license includes vision, knowledge and skills tests except the moped license.

narration.text: Every license rests on tests. In this unit you will learn which tests an original license or a class upgrade requires, which license is the exception, what the knowledge test covers, and the conduct rules that can fail you before you even finish. You will also meet the One Stop third-party testers, learn that the SCDMV may ask for a second skills test, and see what the examiner is really doing in the car. Knowing the rules in advance takes much of the stress out of test day. Each rule here is simple on its own, and together they make test day predictable.

lines.text: Original license or upgrade: three tests

narration.text: An original license or an upgrade to a different class requires vision, knowledge and skills tests, and the vision and knowledge tests can be taken at any SCDMV branch. Every first license includes all three tests except the moped license, which needs only the vision and knowledge tests. A skills test is required for anyone who does not hold a valid driver's license, and the manual uses the names skills test and driving test for the same exam. So if you hear either name, it means the same behind-the-wheel test. Plan your visit around which tests you still need to pass.

lines.text: Leaving early, talking, notes or devices

narration.text: A common mistake is treating the knowledge test casually. The rules are strict. You fail the knowledge test if you leave the test area before finishing, talk to anyone, or bring in written material or any electronic device such as a phone, laptop or tablet. None of these is a warning offense; each one means failure. Before you start, put your phone and notes away outside the test area, plan to stay until you finish, and keep your attention on your own screen without speaking to anyone. A single slip, such as checking a phone, ends the test right there.

lines.text: The examiner will not trick you

narration.text: One Stop Driver Training and Testing Programs, also called third-party testers, may give the knowledge test, the skills test or both for a first-time Class D permit or license and a Class M license. The SCDMV may also randomly select an applicant to pass the skills test again before the license is issued. During the skills test, the examiner rides along only to confirm that you can control the vehicle and obey the rules of the road, and will not try to trick you. Drive the way you practiced. Steady, careful driving is exactly what the examiner wants to see.

lines.text: First licenses and the skills test

narration.text: Here is a quick check: among all first licenses in South Carolina, which one does not require a skills test? The answer is the moped license. Every first license includes vision, knowledge and skills tests except the moped license, which needs only the vision and knowledge tests. If you are applying for any other first license, plan for all three. An original license or an upgrade to a different class also requires the full set, with the vision and knowledge tests available at any SCDMV branch. Plan your study and your test appointments around that difference.

To close, an original license or a class upgrade needs vision, knowledge and skills tests, and only the moped license skips the skills test. The knowledge test covers laws, signs and safety rules, and you bring corrective lenses for the vision test. Leaving early, talking or bringing notes or devices fails the knowledge test. One Stop testers may give the tests for a first-time Class D or Class M license, the SCDMV may ask for a random retest, and the examiner simply confirms safe, lawful driving. Prepare for each of these points and test day holds few surprises.

why_how.text: The test vehicle must be safe and equipped, or the test does not happen.
Knowing what to bring and which tasks to expect helps you prepare.

scenario.text: Chris arrives for the skills test, but the borrowed car's horn does not work.

reasoning.text: A working horn is required, and an unsafe vehicle gets the test postponed.

result.text: Chris's test is postponed, not failed, and Chris can return with a safe vehicle.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a missing seat belt only postpones the test like an unsafe vehicle does.

correction.text: An unsafe vehicle postpones the test, but not wearing your seat belt is an automatic fail.

prompt.text: What happens if you do not wear your seat belt during the skills test?

rationale.text: Not wearing a seat belt during the test is an automatic fail, while an unsafe vehicle only postpones it.

narration.text: The skills test is the last step before a license, and preparation decides much of the outcome. You provide the vehicle, and it must be safe and fully equipped. You also bring certain documents and people, and you should know which tasks the examiner may ask for. In this unit you will learn the equipment list, the difference between a postponed test and a failed one, what to bring, who may be in the car, and the driving tasks that may appear. Walk through this list before your appointment. A short checklist the day before is the best preparation of all.

You must provide the skills test vehicle, and it must be safe. Its headlights, brakes, windshield wipers, mirrors and speedometer must all work. The vehicle also needs working safety belts, turn signals, defroster and horn, plus a valid license plate, registration card and insurance card. Check every item yourself a day ahead, because a single dead bulb or missing card can stop the test before it starts. Treat the list as a pre-trip inspection, the same habit you will use for the rest of your driving life. If any item fails, fix it before the appointment rather than on test day.

Here is a distinction that matters. If the vehicle is unsafe, for example a broken horn or a missing insurance card, the skills test is postponed. You have not failed; you come back with a safe vehicle. But if you do not wear your seat belt during the test, that is an automatic fail. Many applicants assume both problems are treated the same. They are not. Fix the car before the appointment, and buckle up before you move, so neither rule costs you a test. Know which problems postpone the test and which one fails it outright.

title.text: What to bring and who rides

lines.text: Old license or permit, licensed driver

narration.text: Bring your old license or permit if you have one, a licensed driver, and liability insurance information from a company licensed to do business in South Carolina. During the test itself, only you and the SCDMV employee testing you may be in or around the vehicle. That means parents, friends and instructors wait elsewhere. The licensed driver you bring is for getting the vehicle to and from the test, not for riding along. Having everything ready keeps the start of the test calm and on time. Plan the trip so the licensed driver can bring you and wait nearby.

Skills test tasks may include working the lights, wipers, signals and four-way flashers, a brake light check, lane changes and turns, and naming signs. You may also be asked to parallel park, back up in a straight line for one hundred feet, park on a hill and perform a reverse two-point turnabout. Practice each task until it feels routine, especially parallel parking and the turnabout. The examiner is checking control and rule-following, so smooth, careful execution matters more than speed. Practicing every listed task builds the confidence the test rewards.

lines.text: What is the result if unbuckled?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: an applicant starts the skills test without fastening the seat belt. What is the result? The answer is an automatic fail. Not wearing your seat belt during the test is an automatic fail, while an unsafe vehicle only gets the test postponed. Buckling up is part of being tested, not a formality. Before you start the engine, fasten the belt and adjust it, and the examiner will see the habit every safe driver needs from the very first moment of the drive. That single habit is the simplest way to avoid an automatic fail.

lines.text: Bring papers, ride with the examiner only

narration.text: To close, provide a safe vehicle with working headlights, brakes, wipers, mirrors, speedometer, safety belts, turn signals, defroster and horn, plus a valid plate, registration card and insurance card. An unsafe vehicle postpones the test, and skipping your seat belt fails it. Bring your old license or permit, a licensed driver and liability insurance information. Only you and the examiner may be in or around the vehicle, and the tasks may include signals, turns, parking, straight backing and a reverse two-point turnabout.
